newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's Sharif invites Blair for early visit.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's Sharif invites Blair for early visit.

text.p: ISLAMABAD, May 3, Reuter - Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif on Saturday invited his new British counterpart Tony Blair to pay an early visit as Islamabad praised his victorious Labour party's policies towards South Asia.
In a congratulatory message to Blair on his taking office after Labour's massive election victory, Sharif also sought to upgrade relations between Islamabad and London.

Extending what he called "the most cordial invitation" for the visit, Sharif said: "An early high level contact will facilitate as well as accelerate the progress in diverse areas of cooperation on which the two countries have been working together."

"While Britain looks to the future aiming at still higher levels of national achievement, we hope that relations between Pakistan and the United Kingdom will also be elevated," he said in the message, whose text was released in Islamabad.
"The prospects of expanded cooperation look excellent given the traditional goodwill and understanding that exists in the Labour Party for Pakistan," Sharif said.

Earlier, a Pakistan Foreign Ministry spokesman said Islamabad was confident that its "traditional ties of deep friendship and understanding (with Britain) will be further reinforced and strengthened now that both countries are led by bold and progressive leaders".
He said Labour had "always taken keen interest in issues affecting peace and stability in South Asia and supported resolution of all issues on the basis of justice and equity".

This seemed to be a reference to a Labour national executive committee resolution in 1995 that said the party, when in power, would help negotiate a peace settlement in the India-Pakistan dispute over the Himalayan region of Jammu and Kashmir.
Blair was quoted by India's Hindustan Times newspaper recently as saying his government would seek to help negotiate an agreement on Kashmir.
India says the issue can be discussed only bilaterally with Pakistan, without the involvement of a third party. Pakistan says outside help would be welcome to help resolve the dispute.
More than 20,000 people have been killed in the Indian part of Kashmir since 1990 when simmering discontent with New Delhi's rule turned into an armed rebellion.
